title: Space & Cosmos Shorts · Episode 2
chapters: Ocean moons: hidden seas of the outer solar system
Reading starlight: what stars are made of

units.t: Space & Cosmos Shorts. Episode two.
In this episode: Shooting stars and meteorites, Ocean moons: hidden seas of the outer solar system, Reading starlight: what stars are made of and Neutron stars and pulsars.
Part one. Shooting stars and meteorites.
Most shooting stars are specks of dust smaller than a grain of rice, yet a few space rocks survive the fall and carry chemistry older than the Sun.
Not really a star.
Lie on your back somewhere dark for half an hour and you will probably see a few shooting stars.
Despite the name, they have nothing to do with stars.
Each one is a piece of rock or dust, often no bigger than a grain of sand, hitting the atmosphere at roughly 11 to 72 kilometres per second.
It heats the air so violently that it vaporises and makes the air glow, usually 70 to 100 kilometres up.
Astronomers use three words.
A meteoroid drifts in space.
A meteor is the glowing streak.
A meteorite is any piece that survives and lands on the ground.
Why showers return.
On most nights you might see a handful of random meteors an hour.
On certain dates each year the count jumps, sometimes to dozens an hour.
These are meteor showers, and they arrive like clockwork because Earth crosses the same streams of debris at the same point in its orbit.
Most streams were shed by comets as they swung past the Sun.
Halley's Comet, for example, feeds two showers: the Eta Aquariids in May and the Orionids in October.
The meteors seem to fly out from one point, the radiant, and the shower is named after the constellation it sits in.
It is a perspective effect, like parallel railway lines appearing to meet in the distance.
Showers for Australians.
Some famous showers favour the north.
The Perseids in August are low or invisible from much of Australia.
Southern observers do better with the Eta Aquariids, peaking in early May, whose radiant rises higher in our pre-dawn sky.
The Geminids, peaking around the middle of December, are among the richest showers of the year.
Unusually, they come from an asteroid called Phaethon rather than a comet.
For any shower, get away from city lights, let your eyes adjust for at least 20 minutes and lie back to take in as much sky as possible.
Counts are usually best after midnight, when your side of Earth faces forward into the debris stream.
Rocks from the sky.
Meteorites come in three families.
Stony ones are the most common, and many are chondrites containing round grains formed in the dust cloud that built the planets about 4.
6 billion years ago.
Iron meteorites are metal chunks, thought to come from the cores of shattered asteroids.
Stony-iron ones mix both.
On 28 September 1969 a meteorite broke up over Murchison in Victoria.
It contains amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, and grains older than the Sun itself.
Very large rocks barely notice the air and blast out craters, like the 880-metre Wolfe Creek Crater in Western Australia.
In 2013 a roughly 20-metre object exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia, and flying glass injured around 1,500 people.
Found a space rock.
Australia's deserts are excellent meteorite hunting grounds.
Dark rocks stand out on pale ground, and the dry climate slows weathering.
Curtin University's Desert Fireball Network uses cameras to photograph bright fireballs so their landing spots can be calculated and fragments recovered.
If you think you have found one, look for a rock that feels unusually heavy for its size, often attracts a magnet and has a thin, dark, glassy crust from melting during its fall.
Real meteorites rarely have bubbly holes.
Most candidates turn out to be iron-rich Earth rocks or industrial slag, nicknamed meteorwrongs.
State museums can often identify specimens, and in some states meteorites legally belong to the state, so check the rules before selling one.
The key idea: A shooting star is a speck of space rock or dust burning up in the atmosphere, and it lands as a meteorite only if part survives.
Part two. Ocean moons: hidden seas of the outer solar system.
Some of the best places to look for alien life may be dark oceans hidden beneath the ice of moons orbiting Jupiter and Saturn.
Hidden seas, tidal heat.
Out past Mars, sunlight is weak and the surface of Jupiter's and Saturn's moons sits well below minus 100 degrees Celsius.
Yet spacecraft show that several of these moons appear to hide global oceans of liquid water beneath shells of ice.
Europa may hold more water than all of Earth's oceans combined.
How does water stay liquid?
Mainly through tidal heating.
These moons follow slightly oval orbits around giant planets, so the pull of gravity changes and squeezes and stretches them.
Like a paperclip bent back and forth, they warm by friction.
Jupiter's Io is the extreme case, the most volcanically active world in the solar system.
Gentler heating, plus heat from radioactive elements in the rock, appears enough to keep oceans liquid under kilometres of ice.
Europa's hidden ocean.
Europa is slightly smaller than our Moon, but its surface is bright white ice crisscrossed by reddish brown cracks, with very few craters.
That means the surface is young and constantly reshaped.
In the late 1990s NASA's Galileo spacecraft measured how Europa disturbed Jupiter's magnetic field, and the best explanation was a salty, electrically conducting ocean under the ice.
The ice shell is thought to be several to a few dozen kilometres thick, over an ocean perhaps around 100 kilometres deep.
Crucially, that ocean probably sits on a rocky seafloor.
Water and rock could react chemically there, as they do around hydrothermal vents in Earth's deep oceans, where life thrives without sunlight.
Enceladus geysers.
Enceladus is only about 500 kilometres across, small enough to fit within the width of Victoria, so scientists expected little.
Then in 2005 NASA's Cassini spacecraft spotted jets of water vapour and ice grains erupting from long cracks near its south pole, nicknamed tiger stripes.
The plumes feed one of Saturn's rings.
Cassini later flew straight through them, essentially tasting an alien ocean.
It found water, salts, carbon dioxide, ammonia and organic molecules.
Tiny silica grains hinted at hot water reacting with rock on the seafloor, and later analysis found phosphorus, an essential ingredient for life on Earth.
Enceladus appears to tick many boxes for habitability: liquid water, chemical energy and the right raw materials.
Titan and Ganymede.
Saturn's Titan is bigger than Mercury and the only moon with a thick atmosphere, mostly nitrogen.
At around minus 180 degrees Celsius, water is rock-hard, but methane and ethane flow as liquids.
Titan has clouds, rain, rivers and seas of liquid hydrocarbons.
In 2005 Europe's Huygens probe parachuted through the orange haze and landed on a damp plain strewn with rounded ice pebbles.
Measurements suggest a water ocean lies deep below.
Jupiter's Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system and the only one known to generate its own magnetic field.
Hubble observations of its shifting auroras suggest a salty ocean beneath the surface.
Callisto may have one too, and oceans are suspected further out, including Triton and Pluto.
Missions and caution.
If buried oceans are common, liquid water may be far more widespread in the universe than on sunlit rocky planets like Earth, greatly increasing the number of places life could arise.
Several spacecraft are on their way.
ESA's JUICE, launched in 2023, will study Jupiter's icy moons and eventually orbit Ganymede.
NASA's Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, will make dozens of close flybys of Europa.
NASA's Dragonfly, a nuclear-powered rotorcraft, is planned to fly between sites on Titan in the 2030s.
Scientists take great care not to contaminate these worlds with Earth microbes, a principle called planetary protection.
That is why Galileo was deliberately plunged into Jupiter in 2003, and Cassini into Saturn in 2017, as their fuel ran low.
The key idea: Several icy moons hide liquid oceans, kept from freezing by tidal heating as their planet's gravity flexes them.
Part three. Reading starlight: what stars are made of.
In 1835 a famous philosopher declared that we could never know what the stars are made of.
Within a few decades, scientists were doing exactly that, using rainbows.
An impossible question.
The French philosopher Auguste Comte, founder of positivism, wanted science to stick to what could be observed.

In 1835 he gave an example of knowledge forever beyond reach: we could study the stars' shapes, distances and motions, but never their chemical composition, since no one could visit them or take a sample.
It seemed reasonable.
Chemistry meant handling substances in a laboratory, and the stars were unreachably far away.
Yet within about 25 years, scientists found a way to identify elements in the Sun from Earth.
Comte's claim is now often quoted as a warning that 'impossible' can be a dangerous word.
The key had already been found, in a ray of sunlight split by glass.
Dark lines in the rainbow.
Isaac Newton showed in the 1660s that a prism splits sunlight into a rainbow, a spectrum.
In 1814, German optician Joseph von Fraunhofer built instruments precise enough to magnify it and found hundreds of thin dark lines, as if exact colours were missing.
He mapped about 570 and labelled the strongest with letters, a system still used.
He could not explain them.
Around 1859 in Heidelberg, physicist Gustav Kirchhoff and chemist Robert Bunsen heated substances in a flame and studied the light through a prism.
Each element gave its own set of bright lines, like a barcode.
Sodium's two yellow lines matched two of Fraunhofer's dark lines.
Cooler gas in the Sun's outer layers absorbs those same colours, so dark lines reveal which elements are present.
Helium, found in sunlight.
During a total solar eclipse in 1868, astronomers studying the Sun's glowing outer layers saw a bright yellow line that matched no known element.
Jules Janssen observed it from India, and Norman Lockyer studied it soon afterwards.
Lockyer, working with chemist Edward Frankland, concluded it belonged to a new element and named it helium, after Helios, the Greek god of the Sun.
Many chemists were sceptical of an element known only from a distant star.
Then in 1895 Scottish chemist William Ramsay detected the same spectral line from gas released by a uranium mineral.
Helium, the second most common element in the universe, had first been discovered 150 million kilometres away.
The method also found two new elements on Earth, caesium and rubidium.
Cecilia Payne's discovery.
In the early 1900s astronomers assumed stars had about the same make-up as Earth's crust, rich in heavier elements like iron.
Cecilia Payne, a young British astronomer who moved to Harvard because women had few prospects in astronomy in England, applied new atomic physics to stellar spectra.
Her 1925 doctoral thesis concluded that stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium, in vastly greater amounts than anyone expected.
The senior astronomer Henry Norris Russell persuaded her to describe the result as almost certainly not real.
A few years later Russell reached the same conclusion himself.
Payne was right: hydrogen and helium make up about 98 percent of the ordinary matter in stars.
Her thesis is now considered among the most important in astronomy.
Colour, temperature, motion.
Spectra hold far more than a list of ingredients.
A star's colour reveals its surface temperature: red stars are relatively cool, around 3,000°C, while blue-white stars can exceed 20,000°C.
In the early 1900s, Annie Jump Cannon at Harvard classified hundreds of thousands of stars by spectrum into the sequence O, B, A, F, G, K and M, from hottest to coolest, which astronomers still use.
Spectra also reveal motion through the Doppler effect.
Light from an object moving away is stretched towards the red end, while light from one approaching is squeezed towards blue.
Measuring these tiny shifts showed that distant galaxies are rushing away from us, the evidence for an expanding universe, and it still helps detect planets around other stars.
The key idea: In 1835 Auguste Comte called the chemistry of the stars forever unknowable, a reminder that 'impossible' is a dangerous word.
Part four. Neutron stars and pulsars.
Imagine squeezing more than the mass of the Sun into a ball the size of a city, then spinning it hundreds of times a second.
City-sized and crushing.
A neutron star is about 1.
4 times the mass of the Sun, yet only around 20 kilometres across, roughly the size of a large city.
A teaspoon of its material would weigh something like a billion tonnes on Earth.
Its surface is thought to be incredibly smooth, with mountains only millimetres tall.
Beneath it, matter is crushed so tightly that most electrons and protons have merged into neutrons.
The core of a massive star fuses elements until it makes iron, which cannot release energy by fusion.
Gravity wins, and the core collapses in a fraction of a second.
The outer layers rebound in a supernova.
A lighter core becomes a neutron star; a heavier one becomes a black hole.
Little green men.
In 1967 Jocelyn Bell, a postgraduate student at Cambridge, noticed a bit of "scruff" on chart paper from a new radio telescope.
It was a signal pulsing with astonishing regularity, about every 1.
3 seconds.
The team half jokingly labelled it LGM-1, for "little green men".
More pulsing sources elsewhere made an alien explanation very unlikely.
The 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics went to her supervisor Antony Hewish and Martin Ryle, an omission many scientists consider unfair.
The sources were rapidly spinning neutron stars.
A collapsing core spins faster as it shrinks, like a skater pulling in their arms.
Magnetic fields channel beams of radiation from the poles, and each time a beam crosses Earth, telescopes record a pulse.
The fastest known spins over 700 times a second.
Extreme magnetars.
Some neutron stars have magnetic fields far more extreme than usual.
Magnetars are estimated to have fields up to around a thousand trillion times stronger than Earth's.
As a magnetar's crust shifts under these enormous stresses, it can unleash sudden bursts of X-rays and gamma rays.
In December 2004 a giant flare from a magnetar called SGR 1806-20, on the far side of our galaxy, was so powerful that it measurably disturbed Earth's upper atmosphere.
Astronomers now suspect that some magnetars are behind fast radio bursts, brief and extremely energetic flashes of radio waves detected from across the universe.
Collisions that forge gold.
Many neutron stars live in pairs, spiralling slowly towards each other.
In 1974 Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor found a binary pulsar whose orbit shrank exactly as Einstein's theory predicts if the pair radiates gravitational waves.
It earned a Nobel Prize in 1993.
On 17 August 2017, detectors caught the gravitational waves of two neutron stars colliding about 130 million light-years away.
Telescopes worldwide, including in Australia, watched the glowing aftermath, called a kilonova.
Its light carried the signature of freshly made heavy elements.
Astronomers estimate that mergers like this have produced a significant share of the universe's gold, platinum and other heavy metals, possibly including some of the gold in your jewellery.
Clocks across the galaxy.
Some millisecond pulsars tick with a regularity that rivals atomic clocks.
Australia has played a big role in studying them, and CSIRO's Parkes radio telescope, Murriyang, has discovered a large share of all known pulsars.
By timing dozens of pulsars over many years, astronomers watch for tiny shared shifts in when their pulses arrive.

In 2023, several international teams, including the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array, reported evidence of a faint background of very long gravitational waves rippling through the galaxy, likely produced by pairs of supermassive black holes.
Pulsars have even been proposed as a galactic GPS.
The plaques on the Pioneer probes and the Voyager records already carry a map of the Sun's position relative to 14 pulsars, a cosmic return address.
The key idea: A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a ball about 20 kilometres across, left behind when a massive star's core collapses.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Which description fits a meteorite?
Answer. A space rock that survives and lands on Earth.
Question two. What mainly keeps these moons' oceans from freezing?
Answer. Heat from tidal flexing by their planet's gravity.
Question three. What lesson is Auguste Comte's 1835 claim often used to illustrate?
Answer. Calling something unknowable can be wrong.
Question four. What is left behind when a massive star's core collapses and the outer layers explode?
Answer. A neutron star or, if heavier, a black hole.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
